claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 1, 2, and 6, reproduce representative parameter editors such as ROME, MEMIT, and MEND on an openly available model such as GPT-J-6B, using public CounterFact and zsRE edit sets from Hugging Face. First evaluate the original success, paraphrase, and neighborhood metrics to determine whether the reported near-perfect results can be reproduced. Then apply a more realistic, preregistered evaluation: unseen paraphrases, multi-hop consequences from MQuAKE or RippleEdits, contradictory and temporally changing facts, unrelated factual queries, WikiText-103 perplexity, and public capability benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and TruthfulQA. Apply randomly ordered streams of 1, 10, 100, and 1,000 edits, checkpointing after each scale; include an unedited model, sham updates matched in norm, and ordinary continued fine-tuning as controls. Repeat across multiple edit samples and seeds, report bootstrap confidence intervals, and define reliability in advance as high edit success and consistency without statistically or practically significant deterioration on locality or capability measures. If original metrics remain near-perfect but expanded evaluations or long edit sequences reveal degradation, this would support the claims that prior results do not survive realistic evaluation and that damage compounds. Stable performance across seeds, benchmarks, and edit counts would weaken those claims, while degradation also seen under sham updates would suggest generic optimization drift rather than knowledge editing specifically. This experiment could be reduced or made unnecessary by public release of editor checkpoints, complete sequential-edit trajectories, and independently replicated results on the same expanded benchmark suite.

To address subclaims 3, 4, and 5, test the proposed geometric mechanism using the same models and successful edits from Experiment 1. Estimate layerwise representation covariance from a large public, unrelated text sample such as WikiText-103 or C4, and eigendecompose it with held-out validation for covariance stability. For every localized weight update, record the induced residual-stream changes and output-logit changes on both edit prompts and thousands of unrelated prompts. Quantify how update components project onto low- versus high-variance covariance eigendirections and whether equal-sized components in low-variance directions produce larger normalized activation changes, output KL divergence, factual-answer changes, or benchmark loss. Establish causality with norm-matched synthetic perturbations aligned separately to low-, middle-, and high-variance directions, plus a geometry-aware editor that suppresses or regularizes low-variance components while preserving edit success. Measure global propagation through effects across unrelated subjects, relations, domains, and layers, and test whether per-edit low-variance amplification predicts later cumulative damage better than update norm, layer, or edit difficulty. Replication across at least two model families and multiple editors would distinguish a general geometric limitation from an implementation accident. Disproportionate effects from low-variance-aligned perturbations, broad off-target propagation, and damage reduction under geometry-aware regularization would support the mechanism; no association, effects confined to edited prompts, or dependence on only one editor would weaken or localize it. Public activation traces, edit deltas, and causal perturbation results spanning several architectures could make a new experiment unnecessary.

To address subclaims 7 and 8, compare the best parameter editor from Experiment 1 with a parameter-free factual-update system built from immutable model weights plus an external retrieval or key-value memory, using the identical CounterFact, zsRE, MQuAKE, and RippleEdits edit streams. Verify that the parameter-free condition truly leaves weights untouched by hashing every tensor before and after all updates, disabling optimizer state, and logging that only the external index changes. Evaluate both approaches on edit success, unseen paraphrases, multi-hop portability, locality, conflicting updates, update reversal, 1-to-1,000-edit accumulation, MMLU/HellaSwag/TruthfulQA retention, and WikiText-103 perplexity. Also measure retrieval failures, performance when relevant evidence is absent or distractors are present, latency, storage, update time, and total compute so that the comparison does not treat retrieval as costless. Include an untouched-model upper baseline, retrieval with an empty index, and oracle retrieval to separate retrieval quality from the model's ability to use supplied evidence. If the parameter-free system has cryptographically unchanged weights while matching or exceeding editing reliability and capability retention at acceptable resource cost, it is a serious alternative rather than merely a fallback; if it succeeds only with oracle retrieval, excessive context, or much higher cost, that conclusion is weakened. If parameter editing is equally reliable and cheaper, the asserted preference for parameter-free updating is not supported. Auditable weight hashes and a comprehensive matched-cost evaluation released by prior work could obviate this experiment.
reference_experiments: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A pre-edit reference plus honest, non-teacher-forced single-edit measurements that reveal whether previously near-perfect scores survive normal generation.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 includes an unedited control, evaluates at the one-edit checkpoint, reproduces representative parameter editors, and adds a stated realistic evaluation with ordinary capability and factual-generation tests. It therefore supplies both the clean reference and the single-edit comparison, even though it uses a different model, datasets, and metric suite.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A validated outcome measurement that combines semantic agreement with an independent deterministic token-level check, so method rankings cannot be attributed to the evaluator's subjective judgment.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set uses several editing and capability metrics, but nowhere requires a paired semantic-versus-deterministic measurement or a comparison of the rankings they produce. It therefore does not test whether the evaluation instrument itself is responsible for the apparent result.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment establishes whether evaluator-dependent semantic scores are corroborated by an independent deterministic token-level measure.
That cross-check is what distinguishes a property of the editing methods from an artifact of the scoring judge.
Proposed experiment 0 reports success, paraphrase, neighborhood, and benchmark outcomes, but it does not specify either this paired cross-check or agreement between the resulting rankings.
A team running the proposed set would therefore fail to learn whether the reference's apparent method ranking is judge-dependent: missing.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct, normalized, layer-comparable test of directional amplification in representation space, including concentration in low-variance directions and its change as edits accumulate.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 estimates a stable representation covariance, projects edit-induced changes into low- and high-variance eigendirections, uses normalized activation and output effects, tests cumulative prediction of damage, and adds norm-matched causal perturbations across model families and editors. The covariance/eigenvector implementation differs from the reference's SVD statistic but tests the same geometric discrimination.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A comparative, multi-scale evaluation of representative weight-changing and weight-preserving update strategies on factual-editing reliability, generalization, locality, and portability as edits accumulate.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 evaluates representative parameter editors over randomly ordered streams from 1 through 1,000 edits with factual success, paraphrase/generalization, neighborhood/locality, multi-hop consequences, and unrelated-query tests. Proposed experiment 2 adds the direct comparison with a weight-preserving external-memory approach on matched edit streams, including conflicting updates, portability, locality, and accumulation. This supplies the discriminating comparison without requiring the reference's exact method count, model list, or benchmark names.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Out-of-target capability evaluations after sequential edits that distinguish collateral damage to general abilities from simple failure to incorporate the requested facts.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 evaluates capability benchmarks and language-model perplexity after the sequential edit checkpoints, with an untouched model and sham-update controls. Proposed experiment 2 repeats capability-retention and perplexity comparisons through 1,000 edits for parameter editing versus the weight-preserving alternative. These tests directly reveal whether editing harms abilities unrelated to the edited facts.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Robustness checks across model scale, knowledge form, fact difficulty, method configuration, and architectural conditions, including investigation of methods that behave differently from the general trend.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set does test several editors, multiple seeds and edit samples, sham and fine-tuning controls, and replication across at least two model families. However, it does not require a larger-model sweep, event-level knowledge, high- versus low-confidence fact strata, or systematic hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity analysis of the exceptional editor. Those omissions leave important alternative explanations unresolved.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment tests whether the observed collapse is an artifact of model scale, knowledge representation, fact difficulty, method configuration, or an exceptional editor's architecture and hyperparameters.

Proposed experiment 0 addresses sampling and seed variation and compares several representative editors, while proposed experiment 1 adds some cross-family and multi-editor replication; proposed experiment 2 adds a matched alternative-system comparison.
None of the proposed experiments requires testing larger models, event-level facts, confidence-stratified facts, or a systematic sensitivity sweep for the editor that does not collapse.

The proposed outcomes could therefore show repeatability in their selected settings but could not distinguish a general limitation from a scale, knowledge-type, difficulty, or configuration artifact; the team would fail to learn how broadly the claim holds: partial.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly tests realistic sequential editing, collateral capability damage, the low-variance geometric mechanism, global propagation, cumulative effects, and whether an actually weight-immutable retrieval system is a viable alternative. It would therefore provide a substantive answer to the central claim. The conclusion would remain less secure because the scoring instrument is not independently validated against a deterministic token-level measure, and the robustness envelope omits larger-scale, event-level, difficulty-stratified, and systematic exceptional-method analyses.
missing: A paired semantic and deterministic token-level evaluation with an explicit ranking/agreement check.
A robustness sweep covering larger models, event-level knowledge, high- versus low-confidence facts, and systematic hyperparameter/architecture sensitivity of the non-collapsing method.
